reasoning: Destination-allowlist egress control for LLM agents is an established, widely-advocated defense (AWS domain-control, Azure Container Apps egress policies, the "Outbound Sandbox" / egress-allowlist-sandbox pattern, and the "Backdoored Tool Use" paper which explicitly lists "outbound egress control" as a mitigation), so the underlying problem of constraining/detecting agent exfiltration at the network layer is well covered. Most directly, the agent-egress-bench/pipelock project already routes agent traffic through a firewall/proxy and runs malicious (block-expected) vs benign (allow-expected) corpora, reporting Containment (recall), false-positive rate (benign breakage), and detection - essentially the proposal's core experiment. The genuinely unexplored slice is the narrow framing of blocked-egress events as a binary anomaly tripwire signal correlated against benign/malign trajectories with an explicit ROC and a cost comparison against semantic monitoring, which I did not find evaluated in a single published work; this is a modest evaluation-style gap on top of heavily trodden infrastructure rather than a novel problem. The closest matching evaluation (agent-egress-bench) is a non-peer-reviewed GitHub corpus and uses broader wire-level scanning, leaving minor gaps, hence "largely addressed" rather than "already solved".

evidence.title: agent-egress-bench: Tool-neutral attack corpus for AI agent egress security
evidence.summary: Routes agent outbound traffic through a security tool (firewall/proxy) and tests 155 cases across 18 categories with malicious (block-expected) and benign (allow-expected) cases. Reports Containment (recall, 80% floor), False-positive rate (benign breakage), Detection, and Evidence. This is essentially the proposal's core empirical study, though wire-level/tool-neutral rather than a pure destination allowlist framed as a tripwire detector with ROC.

evidence.title: pipelock: Open-source AI agent firewall for MCP security and agent egress
evidence.summary: A mediating HTTP/MCP/A2A/WebSocket proxy that scans agent outbound traffic for exfiltration, SSRF, and prompt injection and emits signed audit receipts. Demonstrates the proposed proxy infrastructure (all agent network calls routed through a mediator that logs/alerts) already exists as working software.

evidence.title: Control which domains your AI agents can access
evidence.summary: Describes deny-by-default destination/domain allowlists for AI agents, restricting outbound connections to trusted destinations and logging connection attempts for audit. Establishes the destination-allowlist egress control as standard recommended practice, though framed as prevention not as an anomaly-detection tripwire with precision/recall.

evidence.title: The Outbound Sandbox: Why AI Agents Need Network-Level Allowlists
evidence.summary: Argues for routing all agent outbound traffic through a local loopback proxy enforcing a domain allowlist, blocking attacker domains and SSRF. A design/threat-model argument with no empirical precision/recall or benign-breakage metrics, framing the allowlist as prevention rather than a tripwire detector.

evidence.title: Your LLM Agent Can Leak Your Data: Data Exfiltration via Backdoored Tool Use
evidence.summary: Demonstrates agent data exfiltration via outbound requests and explicitly lists 'outbound egress control' among mitigation directions, but does not empirically evaluate an allowlist-as-tripwire detector with precision/recall/ROC.

evidence.title: Silent Egress: When Implicit Prompt Injection Makes LLM Agents Leak Without a Trace
evidence.summary: Characterizes covert exfiltration attacks via implicit prompt injection but focuses on the attack; it does not evaluate a destination-allowlist egress firewall as a tripwire detector or report precision/recall, benign-task breakage, or ROC for such a control.
